question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a COMPLETE hydatidiform mole from a PARTIAL hydatidiform mole?

answers.text: Complete mole: 69,XXY karyotype; contains fetal tissue; partial mole: 46,XX karyotype; no fetal tissue

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is reversed. Complete mole has a diploid (46,XX or 46,XY) androgenetic karyotype. Partial mole has a triploid karyotype (69,XXY or 69,XXX).

answers.text: Complete mole: 46,XX androgenetic karyotype; no fetal tissue; snowstorm ultrasound; partial mole: 69,XXY triploid; fetal/embryonic tissue present

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Complete mole arises from fertilisation by two sperms of an enucleated ovum (or duplication of a single sperm) — all DNA is paternal. No embryo is formed. Partial mole has a triploid karyotype (one maternal + two paternal haploid sets) and may contain fetal tissue.

answers.text: Complete mole: higher risk of choriocarcinoma (50%) than partial mole; partial mole: rarely progresses to GTN

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The malignant potential is correct in direction but the figures are wrong. Complete mole: ~15-20% risk of post-molar GTN (not 50%). Partial mole: ~1-5% risk. Neither figure is 50%.

answers.text: Complete mole: triploid; partial mole: diploid androgenetic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is reversed. Complete mole = diploid androgenetic (46,XX); Partial mole = triploid (69,XXY/XXX/XYY).

overallFeedback.feedback: Key comparison: Complete = diploid (46,XX) androgenetic, no fetus, classic snowstorm. Partial = triploid (69,XXY), may have fetal tissue, lower GTN risk than complete.
Well done. Complete mole = 46,XX androgenetic, no fetus, snowstorm USS. Partial mole = triploid 69,XXY, may have fetal parts, higher-risk partial if fetal parts present.
